args.title: plan-deviation-report.docx
args.body:
PLAN DEVIATION REPORT
Bankruptcy Restructuring — Committee Redline vs. Debtor's Original Plan of Reorganization

Prepared: [Date]
Matter: Analyze Counterparty Markup of Plan of Reorganization
Practice Area: Bankruptcy Restructuring

---

I. INTRODUCTION AND SCOPE

This deviation report compares the creditors' committee's redlined Plan of Reorganization against the debtor's original plan, as transmitted with the valuation summary, transmittal email, and disclosure statement excerpts. Its purpose is to identify, categorize, and reconcile every deviation introduced by the committee's markup and to recommend the firm's position on each.

The analysis below reconciles the counterparty markup against the base materials, the disclosure schedules and exhibits, and controlling deal-team correspondence. It integrates the operative instruction set that governs the negotiation posture for each deviation.

---

II. STRUCTURE OF ANALYSIS

Each deviation is analyzed in four parts: (A) the original plan provision; (B) the committee's redline change; (C) reconciliation against the disclosure schedules, exhibits, and controlling correspondence; and (D) recommended position and drafting implications.

The deal-team correspondence controls the negotiation posture. As reflected in the latest partner message, the client will concede the basket conversion but treats any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue. The deliverable reflects that controlling instruction, not any superseded priority ordering in earlier messages in the thread.

---

III. DEVIATION 1 — INDEMNIFICATION CAP REDUCTION AND BASKET CONVERSION
(Deductible to Tipping Basket)

A. Original Plan Provision

The debtor's original plan established an indemnification cap and a claims basket structured as a deductible. Under the deductible structure, the indemnifying party bears all losses up to the basket amount with no recovery by the indemnified party until cumulative losses exceed the basket threshold; once the deductible is reached, recovery is limited to losses in excess of the basket.

B. Committee's Redline Change

The committee's markup silently reduces the indemnification cap and converts the basket from a deductible to a tipping basket. Under a tipping basket, once the cumulative loss threshold is reached, the indemnifying party becomes liable for the full amount of losses from the first dollar (i.e., including losses below the basket threshold), not merely the excess over the basket.

Combined with the cap reduction, the committee's markup materially increases the indemnifying party's exposure by (i) lowering the ceiling on the indemnifier's protection and (ii) increasing the indemnified party's recovery on claims that cross the basket threshold.

C. Reconciliation

Schedule 5.2 of the disclosure schedules lists retained liabilities that the markup's indemnification changes would silently shift. Specifically, the scheduled retained liabilities—which the debtor's plan assigned to the debtor's estate—would, under the committee's combined changes, become recoverable against indemnification obligations because the tipping‑basket mechanism retroactively exposes losses beneath the old deductible threshold.

The schedules and exhibits note that scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials. Accordingly, the identification of listed retained liabilities in Schedule 5.2 means those liabilities may not be reallocated by way of the indemnification mechanism without express, itemized negotiation.

D. Recommended Position

Per the controlling deal-team correspondence, the client will concede the basket conversion (i.e., the shift from a deductible to a tipping basket). Because this concession is expressly granted, the firm should accept the basket conversion as a negotiated point.

However, the reduced indemnification cap is a separate and distinct change. The controlling correspondence does not concede the cap reduction. Because the cap reduction combines with the basket conversion to materially alter the risk allocation in a manner not contemplated by the disclosure schedules, the firm should reject the cap reduction and require restoration of the original cap.

Drafting implications: If the basket conversion is accepted, ensure the indemnification cap—as set forth in the original plan—remains intact. The tipping‑basket mechanism should be implemented so that Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities are not swept into indemnification recoveries beyond the original cap.

---

IV. DEVIATION 2 — MATERIAL ADVERSE EFFECT (MAE) DEFINITION:
ADDED REGULATORY ACTION CARVE-OUTS

A. Original Plan Provision

The debtor's original plan defined "Material Adverse Effect" without carve-outs for regulatory action, consistent with the standard definition that excludes ordinary-course regulatory developments but retains material adverse regulatory changes within the scope of an MAE.

B. Committee's Redline Change

The committee's markup adds carve-outs to the definition of "Material Adverse Effect" for regulatory action of exactly the kind at issue in this matter. In other words, the committee seeks to exclude from the MAE definition the specific category of regulatory developments that are most material to the current circumstances of the debtor.

C. Reconciliation

Schedule 3.7 of the disclosure schedules discloses two pending regulatory inquiries that intersect the markup's proposed MAE carve-outs. These are not hypothetical or generic regulatory exposures; they are specific, pending inquiries known to the parties before the plan was proposed.

The disclosed Schedule 3.7 items are precisely the regulatory actions the committee's carve-out would exclude from the definition of "Material Adverse Effect." Under the general rule that scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials, these pending regulatory inquiries are material facts that the carve-out cannot be permitted to negate.

By carving out regulatory action of the exact kind disclosed in Schedule 3.7, the markup effectively neutralizes the MAE protection for the very risks that the schedules identify as material.

D. Recommended Position

The firm should reject this deviation. The MAE carve-out for regulatory action is not a neutral, standard provision; it is a targeted attempt to insulate a known and disclosed material risk from consequence. The pending regulatory inquiries in Schedule 3.7 are the operative, identified risks, and the carve-out would strip the MAE definition of meaning in precisely the context where it matters most.

The deal-team correspondence does not authorize any concession on the MAE definition. The carve-out should be struck from the committee's redline and the original MAE definition restored.

Drafting implications: ReinsStated the original MAE definition without the regulatory-action carve-out. If the committee presses the point, the alternative fallback position is to narrow or delete the Schedule 3.7 disclosures, but that would require affirmative agreement from the debtor on the materiality of the pending inquiries, which the debtor's plan does not support.

---

V. DEVIATION 3 — LIMITATION PERIOD SHORTENING SURVIVAL
FOR CORE REPRESENTATIONS

A. Original Plan Provision

Exhibit B to the disclosure schedules sets the survival matrix for representations, warranties, and covenants under the debtor's original plan. The matrix specifies distinct survival periods for different categories of representations, including the core representations (e.g., fundamental representations, tax representations, and environmental representations) that typically carry longer survival periods.

B. Committee's Redline Change

The committee's markup introduces a new limitation period that shortens the survival for the core representations. This would compress the survival window for the representations that the plan assigns the longest periods, thereby limiting the period during which a party may assert claims for breach of those representations.

C. Reconciliation

The committee's limitation-period change directly contradicts Exhibit B's survival matrix. The schedules and exhibits expressly state that scheduled exceptions—including the Exhibit B survival matrix—control over general statements in the base materials. The committee's markup does not amend Exhibit B itself; instead, it introduces a general limitation period in the operative text of the plan that conflicts with the schedule.

Because Exhibit B controls, the committee's limitation-period change is inconsistent with the controlling disclosure schedules. The change cannot survive by operation of a general plan provision when the exhibit to the schedules was specifically negotiated to define the survival framework.

D. Recommended Position

Per the controlling deal-team correspondence, any survival-period reduction is a walk-away issue for the client. The deal team has instructed that this particular deviation is non-negotiable.

The firm should treat the survival-period reduction as a material non-starter. The client's position is that this change—alone or in combination with other deviations—cannot be accepted under any circumstance.

Drafting implications: The committee's limitation-period change must be rejected outright. The Exhibit B survival matrix should be preserved in full. If the committee insists on this provision, the negotiation should be escalated to the deal team with a recommendation to terminate discussions rather than accept the reduced survival period.

---

VI. CATEGORIZATION OF DEVIATIONS

The three deviations identified above can be categorized by severity and posture:

1. Indemnification cap reduction — REJECT (cap reduction); CONCEDE (basket conversion)
   - Severity: Moderate-to-High
   - The basket conversion is a permitted concession per deal-team instruction.
   - The cap reduction is not authorized and should be rejected.

2. MAE regulatory-action carve-outs — REJECT
   - Severity: High
   - Conflicts with Schedule 3.7 disclosures; targeted carve-out negates known material risks.

3. Survival-period reduction for core representations — REJECT (WALK-AWAY)
   - Severity: Critical
   - Contradicts Exhibit B survival matrix; deal team designates as a walk-away issue.

---

VII. SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDED POSITIONS

| # | Deviation | Original Provision | Committee Change | Recommended Position |
|---|-----------|-------------------|-------------------|---------------------|
| 1a | Basket structure | Deductible | Tipping basket | CONCEDE (per deal team) |
| 1b | Indemnification cap | Original cap | Reduced cap | REJECT |
| 2 | MAE definition | No regulatory carve-out | Adds regulatory-action carve-out | REJECT |
| 3 | Survival period | Exhibit B matrix | Shorter limitation period | REJECT (walk-away) |

---

VIII. CONCLUSION

The committee's redlined plan introduces three substantive deviations from the debtor's original plan. One component—the basket conversion—is authorized for concession by the client. The remaining changes—the indemnification cap reduction, the MAE regulatory-action carve-outs, and the survival-period reduction—should be rejected.

The cap reduction materially shifts risk in combination with the basket conversion. The MAE carve-out targets precisely the known regulatory risks disclosed in Schedule 3.7. The survival-period reduction contradicts the controlling Exhibit B survival matrix and has been designated by the client as a walk-away issue.

The firm's negotiation posture should be: accept the basket conversion; hold firm on the indemnification cap; reject the MAE carve-outs; and treat the survival-period reduction as grounds to terminate the negotiation if the committee does not withdraw it.

---

P RIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT
Prepared for internal use in connection with the bankruptcy restructuring matter.
